body: The denial is cached even when it comes from stale data other than permissions. `checkInheritedPermissions` uses `buildFolderTree`, which is served from `folderCache` (30s TTL) and never refreshed on a miss. Take a user who has access to folder A and creates subfolder B, then a dashboard in B. The cached tree doesn't know B, so `tree.Ancestors(B)` yields nothing and the request is denied. The DB requery only reloads permissions, not the folder tree, so the result is still a deny, and that deny now goes into `permDenialCache`. For the next 30s every check on that resource short-circuits to deny, so the user can't reach the resource they just created, which is the bug this PR is meant to fix. Consider refreshing the folder tree on a miss before denying, or not caching denials that went through the inherited-permission path.

The denial cache is checked before anything else and is never invalidated. If a Check on a resource runs just before the creator's permissions are written (for example, a get/read issued during or right after a create, before the managed permission is persisted), that denial is cached for shortCacheTTL. Every later Check then returns deny without looking at the refreshed permissions. This re-creates the 'creator can't access what they just created' window this PR is trying to close. The denial cache needs invalidation when permissions change, or a much shorter TTL.

Two problems with this key:
1. It doesn't include the identity type. `validateSubject` returns only the raw id, so `anonymous:0` and `render:0` (or any two identity types sharing an id) produce the same denial key. A denial cached for the anonymous user would then deny the renderer, which has broad permissions, on the same resource.
2. Fields are joined with `_`, but names and folder UIDs can contain `_`. For example, (name=`a_b`, parent=`c`) and (name=`a`, parent=`b_c`) map to the same key, so a denial on one wrongly denies the other.

The key also shares the `.perm_<uid>_<action>` prefix with `userPermCacheKey` in the same underlying cache, which invites collisions with the `map[string]bool` entries. Use a distinct prefix (e.g. `.perm_denied_`), include the identity type, and use a separator that can't appear in UIDs, or encode the components.

This is a performance regression for denials. Before, a denied Check was answered from `permCache`. Now any Check that the cached permissions deny, and that isn't already in the denial cache, triggers a full `getIdentityPermissions` DB query. `getUserPermissions` no longer checks `permCache`, so it always hits the permission store and rewrites the cache. A request that checks many distinct resources the user can't see (search results, bulk list+check filtering, or a caller probing names) now does one permission DB query per distinct (name, folder), and singleflight only merges concurrent calls. It also adds an unbounded number of per-resource denial entries to the shared cache. Consider rate-limiting the requery, e.g. requery at most once per user/action per short interval, instead of once per denied resource.

Nit: `userPermCacheKey` uses `userIdentifiers.UID`, but the denial key uses the raw `checkReq.UserUID`. That can be a numeric id or a UID for the same user, so the two caches are keyed inconsistently. Also, errors from `getCachedIdentityPermissions` other than not-found (such as a `GetUserIdentifiers` DB failure) are silently ignored here and the lookup is simply retried below. That works, but it doubles the DB work when the store is failing.

With the in-proc client cache turned off, every Check/List from the API server now makes a gRPC round trip, even in-proc, and goes through the server's Check logic, which after this PR can hit the DB on every denial. This is a large increase in load for denial-heavy paths. Please confirm this is acceptable, or keep a short-lived client cache for positive results only. Also, `NoopCache` is exported from the `authz` package with receivers named `lc`. It's better unexported, or taken from authlib if authlib already provides a no-op cache.
